sentences.text: This angel has just been thrown out of heaven, and he is looking at you.
This is The Fallen Angel, painted by Alexandre Cabanel in 1847.
It shows the Devil, and he has no horns.
Cabanel painted him as a young man with wings.
Young, handsome, still winged.
But look at his face.
He's weeping.
There's one tear at the corner of his eye.
And yet the brow above it is pulled down hard.
Look into his eyes.
There's rage in there.
A silent, clenched, weeping rage.
As if he has already made up his mind.
According to the Christian story of the fall, God expelled this angel from heaven, and he became the Devil.
And Cabanel, at twenty-four, chose a subject French painters rarely touched.
Not the fall itself, but the hour after it, on the ground.
The moment when the other angels still fly overhead, and he does not.
Imagine being thrown out of the only home you had.
Would you ask to come back?
Would you bow your head and wait?
Or would you swear to make them pay?
That's what makes this painting hard to look at.
The angel is still beautiful, but his eyes no longer look kind.
The tear says one thing, the stare says another.
Maybe this is how the Devil looked on his first day.
Maybe it starts with being thrown out, then a tear, then a decision.
So look at him one more time.
Do you see an angel crying for what he lost?
Or the Devil, one hour old?
